title: Crash with many objects with geoCoordinates props: "panic: runtime error: makeslice: len out of range"
body:
I have had an issue where the weaviate server crashes (and is unable to recover) when I attempt an import of a postcode file that is publicly accessible at https://<redacted-host>/open-postcode-geo

On my system, their error occurs after around 88,000 records have been processed, but this varies. I have had it work fine once (when my docker volume wasn't mapped) and it has failed twice (when my volume was mapped).

I attach the Jupyter notebook which contains the schema definition and file import code.
[PopulatePostcodes.ipynb.zip](https://github.com/semi-technologies/weaviate/files/10435263/PopulatePostcodes.ipynb.zip)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Note for the person investigating this: As mentioned already during the discussion on Slack, an early suspect here could be the `geoCoordinates` prop. We have a lot of large-scale tests, including manual ones up to billion scale that haven't produced this error. But if we can get it to crash with such a small data set, the one thing that immediately stands out to me is the `geoCoordinates` prop. Maybe it has something to do with it.

Good news, everyone!
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8974479/212972485-6a450601-00e0-4491-92e5-2d62f799d93d.png)

I just ran your notebook and I'm getting the same weird behavior. It is indeed related to the index for the geo property. I did not get the exact error message you got, but I got similar nonsense array data. In my case it wasn't out of range, but rather a number that was so big that Weaviate kept allocating memory until it was OOM-killed. 

Thanks, we'll take it from here and hopefully have a fix ready soon!

comments.body:
It seems to initally go wrong with the commit log merge on the `geoCoordinates` prop's HNSW index (geo indexes are also backed by HNSW, just like vector indexes):


comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Thanks. This seems to have fixed it for me as well. Imported all 1.7 million rows whereas previously was crashing out after 90 thousand or so. I had managed to work around the problem with the previous docker images by putting a time.sleep(10) call in my import loop allowing my import to "take a breather" every few thousand records. Does this tally with the fix that you made? Something along the lines of buffers not having enough time to flush or similar?

My bigger concern is not so much with the crash, but with the fact that the database was left in a broken state from which it tried but failed to recover. In a test scenario the solution was to trash the data and retry. If this had been a production system I'd have had a very serious headache. Are there things that can be done when the automatic recovery fails?

Anyway, thanks for the speedy fix.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I did a bit more digging and I'm starting to understand why we never ran into this with a test pipeline before. I tried to add a new test pipeline (independent of your reproducing example) and the pipeline got to 2M objects without a single crash with v1.17.1. So I started comparing the two and it seems that the open-postcode dataset contains a lot of duplicate geo coordinates. The HNSW index isn't very good at handling duplicates, so it has to do a lot more work. That additional work made the race much more likely to happen.

I changed my test pipeline from 2M unique data points to repeating the same 20 or so data points over and over again and the crash happened in the first minute. 

> My bigger concern is not so much with the crash, but with the fact that the database was left in a broken state from which it tried but failed to recover. 

Yeah, the crash was a side-effect of the file corruption. With the corruption fixed, both issues are gone.

> Are there things that can be done when the automatic recovery fails?

Yes, but in this case, some data loss would have occurred because Weaviate was actively "sabotaging" the state on disk. The objects themselves would have been recoverable, but the index for the location points would have been unrecoverable. So if this had been a prod situation, you could have deleted the index, then weaviate would have started up again, and you could have recovered your data, but would still have had to reimport to re-build the index.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: By the way, future releases will have to go through an automated stress pipeline that prevents this. We already had those in place for "regular" properties. But not for `geoCoordinates` props. That will be added now. Better late than never ;-)
